discovery: Quantum simulation of Hubbard models with ultracold atoms in optical lattices, from the superfluid-to-Mott-insulator transition to single-site-resolved quantum gas microscopy

nominees.name: Peter Zoller
nominees.affiliation: University of Innsbruck and IQOQI, Austrian Academy of Sciences, Austria

nominees.name: Immanuel Bloch
nominees.affiliation: Max Planck Institute of Quantum Optics and LMU Munich, Germany

subfield: Atomic, molecular and optical physics / quantum many-body physics
motivation: Feynman proposed simulating quantum matter with controllable quantum systems. Ultracold atoms in optical lattices made this real. Jaksch, Zoller and coworkers (1998) showed that atoms in light crystals realise the Bose-Hubbard model and predicted a Mott transition. Bloch and Greiner observed the superfluid-to-Mott-insulator quantum phase transition in 2002, turning a textbook condensed-matter model into a tunable laboratory system. Greiner (Harvard) and Bloch (MPQ) then invented the quantum gas microscope, which images and controls single atoms on individual lattice sites. This enabled direct observation of Mott shells, antiferromagnetic correlations in the Fermi-Hubbard model, entanglement entropy and many-body localisation. Zoller's theory, from lattice models to synthetic gauge fields and analog simulators, shaped the field conceptually. Together their work founded analog quantum simulation, which now bridges atomic physics, condensed matter and quantum information and underpins neutral-atom quantum computing.
